question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of biopsy-proven cirrhosis attributed to genetically confirmed hereditary hemochromatosis was escorted by his partner to the hepatology same-day access clinic at 10:20 this morning because over the past week he had misplaced the television remote three times in one evening, required extra seconds to calculate the tip at a restaurant, and yesterday drove past the entrance to his own street before realizing the error; the partner also thought his speech sounded slightly slowed and noted a mild, irregular tremor of his outstretched hands while they prepared breakfast. The patient acknowledged feeling “a bit foggy” and reported that for the last month his belt notch advanced one hole by nightfall even though his weight on the home scale had not changed; he described a vague sense of abdominal fullness when tying shoes but denied frank pain, early satiety, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, pruritus, dark urine, clay-colored stools, leg swelling, dyspnea, orthopnea, chest pain, palpitations, lightheadedness, syncope, fever, or chills. He has never bled from esophageal varices, has not undergone therapeutic paracentesis, and has never been prescribed lactulose, rifaximin, non-selective beta-blockers, diuretics, vitamin K, or albumin infusions. His medical background is otherwise significant for well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, stage 1 hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg each morning, and primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine 75 µg daily; there is no history of renal insufficiency, pulmonary disease, cerebrovascular events, or prothrombotic disorders. He underwent phlebotomy every two weeks for the first two years after diagnosis but has required only maintenance sessions every four months for the past five years, the most recent performed six weeks ago. He quit alcohol completely eleven years ago after counseling, has never smoked cigarettes, and denies illicit drug use. Surgical history is notable only for laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair two decades ago, and he has no known drug allergies. His father died of congestive heart failure at 74, a brother has psoriasis, and no relatives are known to have liver disease. He is retired from construction work, walks his dog a mile most mornings, and lives in a single-story house with his partner. Upon arrival—before intravenous access, imaging, medications, or venipuncture—vital signs were temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats/min in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. The man sat upright but buttoned his shirt unevenly by one hole; he oriented to person and place promptly yet paused six seconds to recall the exact date, recited the months forward without difficulty but hesitated reversing them, and displayed a low-amplitude, irregular flap within four seconds when asked to extend arms with wrists dorsiflexed. Speech was coherent though slightly slowed; mood appeared neutral. Breath carried a faint sweet odor. The constellation of subtle cognitive slowing, brief difficulty with date recall, and presence of an asterixis indicates an early, low-grade hepatic encephalopathy. Sclerae were lemon-tinged, conjunctivae pink, oral mucosa moist, and there were three spider telangiectasias on the upper chest with mild palmar erythema; no bruises, caput medusae, or digital clubbing were seen. Neck was supple with jugular venous pulsation at 6 cm H₂O while reclining 30°. Cardiac examination revealed a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear bilaterally. Inspection of the abdomen showed slight distension with the umbilicus still inverted; the abdominal wall moved symmetrically, and no surgical scars were present. Percussion was tympanitic centrally and yielded a narrow crescent of dullness along each flank that shifted subtly when he rolled to the opposite side; a barely perceptible fluid impulse traversed the midline despite the examiner’s static palm. Palpation disclosed a firm, nodular liver edge 1 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, non-tender; the spleen tip was not felt. Bowel sounds were normoactive, and there was no pedal edema. Finger-stick glucose measured 108 mg/dL. Five minutes later, a 21-gauge antecubital venous sample was drawn—documented prior to any fluids, vitamin supplementation, antibiotics, sedatives, or osmotic laxatives—and the initial laboratory panel returned: total bilirubin 2.13 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.88 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 41 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 69 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 132 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 189 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.6 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 118 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.59. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained immediately afterward displayed normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with a QTc of 428 ms; upright postero-anterior chest radiography showed clear lung fields with mildly elevated hemidiaphragms. Point-of-care abdominal ultrasonography performed at the bedside—still before any therapeutic intervention—revealed a small, shrunken, heterogeneously echogenic liver with an irregular capsule, patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 17 cm/s, a spleen length of 15.5 cm, and a thin anechoic stripe of fluid measuring up to 1.8 cm in depth along the right paracolic gutter and pelvis, without loculations. The limited volume of free intraperitoneal fluid on exam and ultrasound is consistent with only a mild, trace ascites rather than a tense collection. Kidneys appeared normal in size and echogenicity, and there was no biliary dilation or focal hepatic mass. Up to the moment this note is finalized, the patient has not received lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, paracentesis, vitamin K, albumin infusion, or antibiotics, ensuring that all observations and laboratory values above reflect his untreated physiologic state at initial presentation while he awaits formal review by the attending hepatologist for discussion of diet, driving safety, and potential initiation of ammonia-lowering therapy.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Child-Pugh assigns 1–3 points each for bilirubin, albumin, coagulation, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. At the untreated visit:
- Total bilirubin 2.13 mg/dL (2–3): 2 points.
- Albumin 3.88 g/dL (>3.5): 1 point.
- INR 1.59 (<1.7): 1 point.
- Ascites: subtle shifting dullness and a thin stripe of free fluid on ultrasound indicate mild ascites: 2 points.
- Encephalopathy: slowed cognition and asterixis without marked disorientation or coma indicate low-grade encephalopathy (grade I–II): 2 points.
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 8 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 8
